description:
Team Helixonauts: 

Five builders across backend, AI, ML and UX. We took on Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions because in space there's no doctor on board. We built HALO, a health check that runs on just a phone camera: it reads heart rate, breathing and blinking, tests alertness with a docking game, compares each astronaut to their own baseline, and guides crews through NASA medical checklists. From the ISS to the Moon and Mars, HALO keeps every crew healthy.
summary:
As missions reach farther from Earth, help from the ground gets farther away. HALO (Health Assistance for Life in Orbit) gives astronauts a fast, private way to know they are fit for the work ahead, using only a phone.
A crew member scans a QR code and completes a short check in the browser. The camera reads pulse, breathing and signs of fatigue, all processed on the device. A brief docking-mission game then tests reaction, attention and memory. In minutes, HALO delivers a clear verdict: ready, caution or rest.

What sets HALO apart is that it knows each astronaut personally. Every result is compared with that person’s own baseline, so small changes surface early. The HALO agent produces daily crew reports and guides emergencies step by step, by voice, while an assistant answers questions on crew health and space weather from live mission data.
HALO also protects crews from their environment. Trained on NASA ISS radiation data, our model caught 93% of radiation peaks 30 minutes ahead on days it had never seen.

HALO is live today as a research prototype. With clinical validation, it can become a trusted companion for every crew, from low Earth orbit to Mars.
details:
HALO is a working prototype for monitoring astronaut health. It combines a phone-based readiness check, a personal baseline agent, a conversational assistant and a radiation forecast in one connected system.

How It Works
A crew member scans a QR code and completes a short check in the phone's browser. The camera measures pulse, breathing, blink rate and eye closure. Then a docking-mission game assesses reaction time, attention, memory and motor control. The check ends with a readiness score and a verdict of ready, caution or rest.

Each result is saved and sent to the HALO agent, which compares it with the crew member's own baseline. The agent produces daily crew reports and runs voice-guided emergency checklists. A conversational assistant answers questions about crew status, lab values, space weather and radiation, using only live mission data. A machine-learning model trained on NASA's ISS dosimeter data forecasts radiation peaks 30 minutes in advance.

Benefits

  • Personalized assessment against each crew member's own baseline
  • On-device processing, so no video leaves the phone
  • No additional hardware required
  • Early radiation warning: 93% of peaks caught on unseen days, about four times as many as a simple threshold rule, with higher precision (82% vs. 65%)
  • Unreliable readings are withheld rather than shown

Intended Impact
As missions travel farther from Earth, real-time support from the ground becomes limited. HALO gives crews a fast way to assess their own readiness and an early warning of environmental risk. A validated version could support long-duration missions and remote, isolated settings on Earth.

Tools and Technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Python
  • Frameworks and libraries: FastAPI, scikit-learn, Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker, Web Speech API
  • Infrastructure: GitHub Pages, Supabase (Postgres), Railway, Twilio
  • Testing: pytest and the Node test runner, with more than 380 automated tests
  • Hardware: standard smartphones
  • Data: NASA OSDR RadLab, DONKI, and OSDR datasets OSD-569 and OSD-575 (Inspiration4)

Creativity
HALO turns an everyday phone into a complete readiness station. The cognitive tests are built into a single docking-mission game. The pulse reading combines three camera methods and accepts a value only when they agree. HALO also brings crew health and the space environment together in one system, with a single assistant for both.

Key Considerations

  • Safety: HALO is clearly labeled as a research prototype, not a medical device, and the assistant gives no medical advice of its own.
  • Privacy and security: Video stays on the device. Access is restricted through row-level security, and no secrets are stored in the code.
  • Data integrity: We used NASA sources only, documented every derived value, corrected a source-data error, and verified that no data leaked between training and testing.
  • Rigor: The model was trained on a period that includes the strongest geomagnetic storm in two decades and tested on days it had never seen.
  • Cost: The whole system runs on free infrastructure.
  • Next steps: We plan to validate the pulse readings against a clinical reference device, test with a wider range of users, and study how orbital conditions affect the camera measurements.
